summary: Proposes an extension to IP addressing to relieve address exhaustion, using an escape mechanism in the IP options field to carry larger addresses without changing the base IP header. It is an informational proposal.

eli5.summary: Instead of building new, bigger mailboxes, this idea adds a note on the side of the old envelope that holds the extra part of a longer address.

subtitle: Using IP options to extend addresses without breaking backward compatibility

tldr.problem: The 32-bit IP address space was rapidly being exhausted in the early 1990s as more networks wanted to connect to the Internet. Changing the IP header to use larger addresses would break all existing implementations and require a new protocol.
tldr.mechanism: Instead of modifying the core IP header, this RFC proposes a Class F escape mechanism that puts part of the extended address in the IP header and the remainder in the options field. Hosts that understand Class F process both parts as a complete address; hosts that do not understand it ignore the datagram, allowing a smooth transition.
tldr.outcome: This was one of several competing proposals for address extension. IPv6 eventually won out with a completely new address format and header structure, making this proposal obsolete.

facts.label: Options space used
facts.value: 4 words (16 octets) of the available 10 words

today: RFC 1365 is Informational and historically obsolete. IPv6 was chosen as the standard extension to the IP address space, providing a completely redesigned 128-bit address space instead of trying to extend IPv4. This proposal was one of several competing ideas in the early 1990s addressing crisis, and IPv6's eventual standardization made it unnecessary.

sections.title: The IP Address Exhaustion Problem
sections.content:
By 1992, the Internet's explosive growth had created an urgent problem: the 32-bit IP address space was nearly exhausted. The IP addressing scheme divides the 32 bits into a network number and a host number, with five address classes. Class A (highest bit 0) has 7 bits for network number and 24 bits for hosts. Class B (bits 10) has 14 bits for networks and 16 for hosts. Class C (bits 110) has 21 bits for networks and 8 for hosts. Class D is reserved for multicast and Class E is reserved.

The problem was that Class A and B addresses were allocated inefficiently. Many organizations held Class B addresses even though they did not need 65,536 host addresses, leaving insufficient large blocks for new networks. Increasing the address size to more than 32 bits would solve the problem, but at the cost of making a new, incompatible IP header definition. Any other approach—such as switching to OSI protocols like CLNP—would take years to implement globally.
sections.eli5: Postal codes were running out because countries got too many new addresses to fit in the old numbering system. Building a completely new postal code system would take decades.

sections.title: The Class F Escape Mechanism
sections.content:
This RFC proposes not to change the IP header itself, but to use an escape mechanism. The proposal redefines Class E (four high-order bits set to 1111) to be more precise as bits 11110, and introduces a new Class F with bits 111110 set as the leading six bits. When a host sees a Class F address in the source or destination IP field, it understands that the address is incomplete and must look in the IP options field to find the remaining address bits.

The IP header's IHL (Internet Header Length) field allows up to fifteen 32-bit words. The minimum header is five words (20 octets), leaving ten words for options. The RFC proposes reserving six words for standard options and using the remaining four words (16 octets) for extended address parts. Each extended address part is in Type-Length-Value format for consistency with other IP options. An Offset field points to where the second part of the address is located, avoiding the need to search through all options.
sections.eli5: The old envelope still has the first part of the address in the normal place. The new part goes in a special note attached to the envelope that newer systems can read.

sections.title: Class F Subclasses
sections.content:
Two main Class F variants are defined. Class F-4 extends addresses from 32 bits to 48 bits total (4 additional octets from the options field), and Class F-8 extends addresses from 32 bits to 80 bits (8 additional octets from the options field). Each is further subdivided into subclasses (F-4A, F-4B, F-4C, F-4D for Class F-4; F-8A through F-8G for Class F-8) that parallel the structure of the original address classes, defining how many bits are used for the network number versus the host number.

For example, Class F-4A has 7 bits for network number and 24 bits for host addresses, mirroring the original Class A structure. Class F-8D reserves 28 bits for network number and 32 bits for hosts, allowing for a much finer granularity of network allocation. Class F-4D and Class F-8D reserve their space for multicast addresses, maintaining backward compatibility with the multicast concept.
sections.eli5: There are different ways to split the extra address bits between network and host numbers, just like with the old address classes.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility and Limitations
sections.content:
If a host does not support Class F addresses, it will not understand a datagram with a Class F destination address and will ignore it. Communication between such a host and a Class F-capable host is not possible, but this is acceptable because it encourages the adoption of Class F support. The changes required are minimal: a receiving host must add a simple bit-masking check to detect Class F addresses and route them to a dedicated Class_F_Processing() procedure, which can be implemented as a separate module.

The key advantage of this approach over a completely new IP header is that old routers and hosts do not need to be replaced immediately. Class F datagrams will simply not reach non-Class F hosts, creating a gradual, market-driven transition. However, the proposal requires new systems to explicitly detect and handle the extended format, whereas a truly transparent extension would be preferable.
sections.eli5: Old post offices don't know how to read the new format, so mail doesn't reach them. But that's okay because we're gradually replacing old post offices anyway.
